description_full: Portland General Electric Company, an integrated electric utility company, engages in the generation, wholesale purchase, transmission, distribution, and retail sale of electricity in the state of Oregon. It operates six thermal plants, four wind farms, and seven hydroelectric facilities. As of December 31, 2025, the company owned an electric transmission system consisting of 1,744 circuit miles, including 287 circuit miles of 500 kilovolt line, 414 circuit miles of 230 kilovolt line, and 577 miles of 115 kilovolt line; 466 miles of 57 kilovolt line; and served 960 thousand retail customers in 51 cities. It also has 29,251 circuit miles of distribution lines. Portland General Electric Company was founded in 1889 and is headquartered in Portland, Oregon.

Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Portland General Electric Co is a mid-cap utilities business with a $5.5B market cap on $3.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +11% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $71M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.0) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent

Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.

sect: Its 16% operating margin trails the Utilities median (21%) by 6pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.81x).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 97 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 8% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 16% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 19% and a beta of 0.38, it is more defensive than the market.
About $68.3M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 2.1x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 45% in the 2020 crash, 25% in the 2022 bear market and 45% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $39.32 (margin of safety -17%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 19%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Utilities peers: EV/EBITDA 10.0 vs 12.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 16% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -1.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $51.00 on average, 11% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 5.7%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.10).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.65x.
ROE of 7% is amplified by 3.2x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.1x net debt to EBITDA ($69.0M of cash against $4.7B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.4x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.96 in the distress zone.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.5% over 3 years, 10.8% over 5 years and 6.5% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 5.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 2.1x depreciation (33.2% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.5%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 7 sales over the past year, net $996K sold.
It returns 4.1% a year to shareholders (4.8% in dividends).
The share count has grown 5.9% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 19 consecutive years, raising it 10.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 2,877 employees, each generates about $1.2M of revenue, 1.2x the Utilities median, and revenue has grown 4.7% a year across its filed history.
Free cash flow is negative, at -$25K per employee.
CEO pay is $2.9M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
